chunks: "A linear motor is basically a rotary motor that's been cut open and rolled out flat, so instead of torque on a shaft you get force along a line.
There's a stationary part, usually a track of alternating magnets, and a moving part, the forcer or slider, which carries the coils.
When you energise the coils in the right sequence, the interaction between the coil currents and the magnet field pushes the slider along the track.
It's the same Lorentz force, F equals BIL , so force is proportional to current and the moving coils generate a back-EMF proportional to speed, just like a rotary motor.
The big advantage is direct drive: no gearbox, lead screw or belt, so no backlash, much less friction and wear, and very high speed and acceleration with good positioning accuracy.

The downsides are cost, heat (no gear reduction means you need high current for force), limited continuous force, strong attraction between iron-core forcers and magnets, and the need for a position sensor like a linear encoder.
Examples: the voice coil that moves a hard drive head, wafer stages in chip manufacturing, high-end pick-and-place machines, and maglev trains."
